newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Sept 3.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Sept 3.

text.p: Prepared by The Broadcast Monitoring Company for Reuters
FINANCIAL TIMES
-- MORGAN GRENFELL FUNDS SUSPENDED

An inquiry has been launched by London regulators into three UK-based investment funds managed by Morgan Grenfell, a subsidiary of Deutsche Bank. The investigation, by the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation, has forced the suspension of all three unit trusts, which hold a combined total of 1.4 billion stg on behalf of 90,000 investors.
-- CONSUMER DEMAND FUELS BIG RISE IN FACTORY OUTPUT

Encouraging figures on factory output issued on Monday have boosted Chancellor Kenneth Clarke's hopes of approaching the next general election from a position of rising economic growth. The figures, revealed in the monthly survey from the Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply, show the biggest rise in factory output and orders since spring last year and signal a steady recovery in manufacturing.
-- SHAKE-UP COSTS 113 MILLION STG AT AEA TECHNOLOGY

A pathfinder prospectus for state-owned engineering and science group AEA Technology, which the government hopes will raise 200 million stg when it is floated later this month, has revealed that radical restructuring has cost the group 113.9 million stg in charges since 1994. Most of the costs are tied to reducing the work force, but the group has also spent 3.1 million stg this year in preparation for the flotation, including fees to advisers.
-- LABOUR TO CALL FOR 'SOCIAL CLAUSE' IN TRADE DEALS

A Labour Party proposal to link international trade to labour standards in the countries involved is set to undermine attempts to portray itself as the party of business. The clause, to be published in a party industry policy document, is against the advice of the Confederation of British Industry and would be opposed by most developing countries.
-- TRADE UNION SET TO SUE ON 'MIS-SOLD' PENSIONS

The UK's largest trade union, Unison, has submitted 150 cases to solicitors in which, it believes, its members have been mis-sold personal pensions. The solicitors will decide whether the union can issue writs against the life companies involved, which include the Prudential, Pearl Assurance, Standard Life and Allied Dunbar.
-- CABLE CHANNELS PROBED OVER 'BUNDLING'

The UK regulator of commercial television, the Independent Television Commission (ITC), is to investigate the "bundling" of cable television channels following a complaint from the cable industry. The practice of bundling together channels is an established marketing strategy in the industry, but the ITC may rule it anti-competitive. The issue was also investigated by the Office of Fair Trading earlier this year.
-- CONDE NAST TO LAUNCH TWO TITLES

Up-market publisher Conde Nast is to add to its stable of magazines -- which currently includes Vogue, Tatler and Vanity Fair -- with the 10 million stg launch of two glossy monthly magazines in the UK. GQ Active will be a British version of a monthly health, fitness and sports magazine for men, with the second title being a UK version of Conde Nast Traveller.
-- GEC AMENDS SIMPSON'S INCENTIVES

GEC has moved to quell unease among institutional investors over the 1.5 million stg pay deal awarded to new managing director George Simpson, by revising the terms of the package and introducing tougher performance criteria for incentive awards. A number of major institutional investors has threatened to vote against Simpson's appointment at GEC's annual general meeting this week.
-- ROVER'S NEW CHIEF FACES LONG HAUL

Rover's new chief executive, Walter Hasselkus, who took control of the loss-making car manufacturer on Monday, has been warned that owners BMW may have to invest heavily in the company and that it could take years to turn around Rover's lacklustre performance. Hasselkus is expected to oversee investment in Rover of 500 million stg a year.
-- BLENHEIM SHARES SLIDE AS TALKS END

Shares in exhibitions organiser Blenheim Group have fallen 16 per cent after an announcement late on Friday that it has ended takeover talks with media and financial services company United News and Media. Shares in Blenheim, which is reported as wanting at least 500p per share, fell 63p on Monday to close at 335p. Some analysts are maintaining that the group could still find a suitor, particularly after it publishes interim results on October 2.
